newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Heated Belgian Renault workers clash with police.
newsitem.headline: Heated Belgian Renault workers clash with police.

text.p: Belgian police on Friday turned water cannon on irate Renault workers who marched in their hundreds through central Brussels in protest at plans to shut down their Belgian car plant.

Noisy protesters, throwing eggs and stones, clashed with police in riot gear as they tried to break through a barbed-wire barricade in front of the offices of the Flemish regional government. The doomed plant is in Flanders.
There were no reports of serious injuries or arrests.

Up to 900 people joined the protest -- with about half the crowd made up of disillusioned workers from bankrupt Belgian steel maker Forges de Clabecq - throwing fire crackers and shouting "Renault must stay open" as they marched.
Organisers had expected up to 5,000 supporters for the protest over Renault's plans to close its profitable assembly plant at Vilvoorde near Brussels with the loss of 3,100 jobs.

But after five weeks of action against the decision workers are losing hope for a reversal of the closure, especially since Renault has failed to give them even the slightest indication it could change its mind.

A small delegation of demonstrators was received by the office of Flemish regional president Luc Van de Brande and by the office of Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, who is on a visit to Latin America.
A spokesman for the Flemish government told them there was little Flanders could do. Any action against French companies might only jeopardise more jobs, he said.
The workers were then due to go to the offices of European Union Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert.

The Renault workers got a moral boost on Thursday when a Belgian court ruled the French carmaker had broken labour law by not consulting properly about its surprise announcement on February 27 to close the Vilvoorde plant in July.
The court, which called on both sides to try to find a way to avoid or reduce the job losses, could fine Renault or have managers jailed if it fails to now fully consult employees.
Renault has said the fact that it failed to follow procedure would not alter its decision to close Vilvoorde to cut overcapacity and costs, and announced it would appeal against the ruling.

In an interview published on Friday in the French newspaper Liberation, Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer said the car maker might close the Vilvoorde plant earlier than the end of July if workers did not resume production.

Vilvoorde workers have been occupying the factory, holding billions of francs worth of finished cars hostage, since the closure announcement and have been joined in protests with colleagues from Renault plants in France and Spain.
"The cars which have been blocked remain blocked. We won't give up our weapon to the management and start back at the beginning again," union representative Georges Jacqmijn told Belgian radio.
Renault -- which lost 5.2 billion French francs ($925 million) in 1996 -- has also announced plans to cut nearly 3,000 jobs in France.
Renault trade unions have called for stoppages on Friday at all the company's European plants.
